title: Ang 340–345: Kabir's letters and days
hookLine: Kabir's own alphabet, lunar days and weekdays
tomorrow: a city with no tax and no fear. who dreamed it up?

cards: It's past midnight. The cursor blinks. The toast is due Friday, and you've typed Welcome, everyone four times and deleted it four times.

Every letter on the keyboard is right there, and none of them will say the thing. On ang 340 of the Guru Granth Sahib, a weaver sits down with the same problem and a far bigger subject. He knows the letters will fail him.
He writes out the whole alphabet anyway. Why?

teach.b: From ang 340, Kabir takes the letters one at a time and hangs a line of teaching on each. The Granth calls it Bavan Akhri, the fifty-two letters, and Kabir names the number himself in its opening lines.
In paraphrase: the three worlds are all described with these fifty-two letters; these letters will wear away; that other Word isn't among them. So the poem begins by admitting it can't do the job.
Every letter after that is an arrow, not the target. A few lessons back we met Guru Arjan's fifty-two letters; this is the weaver's version, shorter and blunter. Then Kabir does the same with time.
On ang 343, his Thiti walks through the days of the moon, and he says, in paraphrase: fifteen lunar days and seven weekdays, and the One has no near shore and no far one.

Then the seven weekdays, one by one, each a reason to sing. Letters, days of the month, days of the week: the things we use to spell and measure everything. Kabir turns each one toward the One it can't hold.
That's the answer to the blinking cursor. The words were never going to contain it.

teach.h: THE WORDS POINT; THEY DON'T HOLD.

teach.b: And pointing is enough to begin.

how: Sikhs reading the Guru Granth Sahib in order, at home or in a sehaj paath, reach Kabir's Bavan Akhri, his Thiti and his weekday hymn near the end of Raag Gauri; some follow along in a Gurbani app with the meaning under each line.

games.q: kabir's letters and days — tap the pairs.

s: Kabir says his letters can capture the One
he says the opposite: these letters will wear away, and that other Word isn't among them.
Kabir also walks through the lunar days and the weekdays
the Thiti from ang 343, then the seven weekdays, each turned toward the One.
Guru Arjan wrote the only alphabet poem in Gauri
Guru Arjan has fifty-two letters in Gauri, and Kabir has his own.

games.q: your friend has to thank her coach at the team banquet and says no words will ever be enough, so she'll skip it. what fits Kabir's alphabet?
o: say it anyway: the words can't hold it all, but they can point.
skip it: if words fall short, silence says it better.
keep drafting until nothing at all is missing.
games.why: Kabir opens by admitting his letters will wear away and can't hold the One, then writes all fifty-two. pointing is enough to begin.

practice: Open ang 340 in a Gurbani app if one is near, and read the opening lines slowly, aloud or under your breath. Then, by hand, write one letter, any letter of any alphabet, on paper or with a fingertip on your palm.
Rest with it for the sit: one small shape doing its best to point at something larger.
